Fiber metal laminates (FMLs) consist of alternating layers of metal sheets and fiber-reinforced composites.
FMLs combine the high bearing strength and impact resistance of metals with the fatigue resistance and high strength-to-weight ratio of composites.
Damage tolerance design must consider impact damage, environmental effects, and fatigue-related damage.
Three approaches to damage tolerance compliance are damage tolerant materials, structural design features, and combined material-structural design.
Composite materials often suffer internal damage without visible surface signs, complicating damage detection.
Quasi-isotropic layups in composites improve in-plane stiffness and strength by orienting fibers in multiple directions.
The Airbus A380 uses Glare FML as the upper fuselage skin, marking a successful aerospace application.
Fatigue crack growth in FMLs can be modeled using linear elastic fracture mechanics similar to metals.
Metallic layers in FMLs improve repairability and damage detectability compared to full composites.
Inspection techniques must detect damage location and severity to reduce operational and maintenance costs.
FMLs have not yet seen widespread adoption beyond specific applications like Glare due to limited experience and certification challenges.
Fiber reinforced polymers are generally corrosion resistant, but galvanic corrosion can occur when combined with metals.
Damage tolerance evaluation must include all relevant damage scenarios for realistic structural weight analysis.
The smart material approach tailors constituent materials and their arrangement for optimal structural performance.
Fatigue damage in composites involves multiple damage modes such as delaminations and matrix cracking, unlike metals.
FML technology readiness has been demonstrated through full-scale applications and testing.
Maintenance and repair costs are significant drivers in material and structural design choices for aircraft.
The combination of metal and fiber layers in FMLs can lead to significant weight reduction in aircraft structures.
Damage detection accuracy depends on damage type, material, and inspection technique.
The fatigue design strain limit for CFRP is typically around 0.35%, much lower than metals.
